title: Ge-free dopant-contrast superlattice (Si / Si:B) for 3D silicon DRAM
idea: 3D silicon DRAM (Samsung VS-DRAM, SK hynix, imec) starts from an epitaxial Si/Si0.8Ge0.2 superlattice whose SiGe layers are later etched out to free horizontal Si channels; imec's 120-bilayer stacks still show dislocations because the 0.84% mismatch accumulates strain, and A2 puts fleet-scale Ge demand at 6-38% of refined supply. Instead grow intrinsic Si alternating with heavily boron-doped Si (1-3e20 cm-3, optionally carbon co-doped, or with ~1-4% Ge to null the small lattice contraction) by the same low-temperature RPCVD. Remove the sacrificial layers through the slit with dopant-selective chemistry: an HF/HNO3/CH3COOH etch that attacks heavily doped Si far faster than intrinsic Si, or selective electrochemical porosification of the p+ layers followed by a fast porous-Si strip. The intrinsic layers become channels; boron tails matter only until the sacrificial layers are gone.
why: Misfit 0.84% -> 0.05-0.16% (strain energy 30-260x lower), so tier count is no longer strain-limited; Ge per wafer 5-16x lower, or zero.

title: Sandwich stack: Smart-Cut single-crystal sense layers every 16 oxide tiers
idea: Build oxide-channel 3D DRAM tiers (horizontal or vertical-channel 1T1C or 2T0C) in groups of 16, then bond a ~50 nm single-crystal Si layer on top by Smart Cut (H-implanted donor, low-temperature bond, split) and build n- and p-channel transistors in it at <=400 C, as CEA-Leti showed with full 2.5 V n&p SOI MOSFETs at 400 C (IEDM 2025, nanosecond laser anneal plus solid-phase regrowth). That layer holds the local sense amps, tier decoders and muxes for the 16 tiers below; the next 16 tiers go on top. Each vertical bitline is only 16 cells tall (~2-4 fF), so a 1T1C cell needs only ~0.3-0.6 fF, which fits in a ~30-60 nm lateral capacitor inside the tier, shrinking the per-tier footprint from A1's ~0.03 um2 base case to ~0.01 um2. Global bitlines run up to a bonded or top-level periphery.
why: In-tier capacitor 600 nm -> 31-59 nm; per-tier footprint ~3x smaller; 64 tiers -> ~4.5 Gb/mm2 (10x 1-beta) and ~5-7x bits/$ before yield.

title: Coaxial 4F2 2T0C: the storage node is the core gate of a read-channel shell
idea: Each cell is one pillar on a 2F x 2F grid. The core is a metal storage node (~20 nm diameter, ~150 nm tall) wrapped by a gate dielectric and an ALD IGZO/IGO shell; the shell is the read transistor's channel and the core is its gate (an inverted channel-all-around device), contacted by a source plane at the bottom and a read-bitline ring at the top. Above the core sits the write transistor: a short vertical oxide channel gated by a write-wordline ring, linking the write bitline at the pillar top to the core. Four line levels (source rows, read-bitline columns, write-wordline rows, write-bitline columns) each run at 2F pitch at different heights, so the 2T0C occupies 4F2 per tier. Tiers stack monolithically at <=400 C over CMOS-under-array.
why: Per-tier density 2.5-3.4x better than A3's 10F2 vertical 2T0C: 1-beta parity at bits x tiers = 4.1 at F = 40 nm (no EUV, no multipatterning) vs 14; 2 bits x 8 tiers at F = 40 nm = 3.9x 1-beta density and ~2.5x bits per wafer-dollar before yield.

title: AAO-Cap: self-ordered anodic-alumina capacitor mold
idea: Sputter a 2.5-3 um Al film over the access-transistor array and its TiN/W landing pads. Nanoimprint shallow pits registered to the pads (Masuda pretexturing), then anodize at ~15-20 V in sulfuric/oxalic acid: pores nucleate at the pits and grow straight down at aspect ratio >=100, stopping at the pad metal; the alumina barrier at each pore bottom is thinned by a voltage ramp-down and removed by a short wet or atomic-layer etch. An ALD Al2O3 liner seals the anion-contaminated pore walls, then TiN / ZrO2-Al2O3-ZrO2 (or the B2-02/B2-03 dielectric) / TiN cup capacitors are ALD-coated inside the pores. The rigid alumina honeycomb stays in place as the mechanical support lattice, so there is no pillar leaning and no SiN support-lattice masks. The bit is stored and sensed exactly as in a 1T1C cell (Si BCAT or IGZO 4F2 VCT access device).
why: Capacitor 2.5-3 um tall (pore AR ~100-115) with no plasma HAR etch: Cs 7.4-8.9 fF at a 4F2 40 nm-pitch cell (+37-64% vs 1-beta's 5.4 fF) at ~1-beta-parity density with periphery under cell; capacitor-hole module goes from ~3 masks + fluorocarbon HAR etch + SiN lattice to 1 imprint + wet anodization (~8 Wh/wafer).

title: Defect-budget co-design: 100x pattern-defect tolerance to unlock cheap patterning
idea: Every 128-bit word carries 16 BCH (t=2) check bits instead of 8 SECDED bits, decoded in fast logic-process periphery (bonded or under-array). A small CAM remaps the few residual failing words found at test; mat-level sparing (NAND bad-block style) handles clustered pattern defects (line opens, shorts). Retention-weak cells are remapped too. This turns patterning defectivity from a yield killer into a few percent of area overhead.
why: Random-defect tolerance x100 (p 1e-6 -> 1e-4) for +6.25% extra check bits and ~65 remap words per 16 Gb die.

title: Weight-streaming DRAM die: few banks, wide rows, no refresh
idea: HBM4 dies carry 256 banks and wide internal datapaths to serve random access from many pseudo-channels. A weight stream instead reads the same addresses in the same order every decode step. A streaming die uses ~16 large banks whose full rows are latched into a row-wide output FIFO and shifted onto TSVs, and a programmable sequencer replaces command decoding and per-bank state machines. It has no REF logic or refresh timers, because use refreshes every row (B4-03), with only a minimal self-refresh for idle. Mats and bitlines can be longer wherever the stream hides latency. It keeps the HBM base-die and TSV interface, so it stacks or sits beside HBM4 and HBF.
why: ~1.3-1.5x less silicon per bit than HBM for the weight-holding share of accelerator memory (array efficiency ~0.36 -> 0.45-0.55), plus zero refresh. It lands between HBM (3x DDR5 wafer/bit) and HBF.

title: 2D-barrier quasi-volatile 1T cell (seconds-to-minutes retention traded for endurance)
idea: A graphene or MoS2 channel sits over an hBN tunnel barrier (2-4 layers) and a floating gate or charge-storage layer (HfO2/Al2O3 or graphene). Fudan's PoX showed 2D-enhanced hot-carrier injection programming in 400 ps at 5 V, with 5.5e6 cycles. Fudan's 2D semi-floating gate showed 10 s retention with ~15 ns writes. The twist is to tune barrier thickness and injection mechanism (direct tunnelling vs hot-carrier) for a DRAM point: retention 10-100 s at 85 C, writes <=10 ns at ~2-3 V, and endurance as the optimisation target rather than retention. The read is non-destructive (gain cell). The cell is 1T, 4F2, BEOL-stackable if 2D films grow on wafers.
why: Refresh 156x (10 s) to 1,562x (100 s) less frequent; 1T 4F2 at F = 20 nm = 0.30 Gb/mm2 per layer (0.67x 1b), multiplied by layers or bits per cell. Endurance must rise 1.8e5x to reach 1e12.

title: Superconducting kinetic-inductance memory with frequency-multiplexed readout (4 K)
idea: Each cell is a NbN (or similar) nanowire loop whose kinetic inductance (~70 pH per square) holds a persistent current; one flux quantum is one bit. Heater cryotrons (hTrons) or nanocryotrons drive a branch normal to write and to read. Row-column arrays exist (MIT and NIST). The twist: each column's sense element is a superconducting resonator at its own frequency on a shared feedline (MKID-style), so thousands of columns read out through one coax and 4 K wiring heat drops sharply.
why: Intrinsic energy per operation is ~1e-20-1e-17 J (I*Phi0 ~2-6e-20 J), against ~fJ for CMOS. Density, however, is only 2.6e-5 Gb/mm2 today (1/17,000 of DDR5) and ~0.005 Gb/mm2 at best (1/90): an L1/L2-class memory for SFQ logic, not a DRAM replacement.

title: Click-RAM: a snap-through 2D-nanoribbon mechanical floating gate over an oxide channel
idea: A ribbon of graphene, monolayer MoS2 or ~2 nm ALD Al2O3/TiN, 50-100 nm long and 10-20 nm wide, is clamped at both ends over a sealed 3.5-6 nm cavity with 0.1-0.3% built-in compressive strain, so it has two stable buckled shapes (+q and -q, q = 1.2-2.3 nm) that never touch the floor. An IGZO (or Si) channel under the cavity is the bottom electrode: a 1.9-2.8 V pulse between ribbon and channel snaps the ribbon down; a pulse on a top plate snaps it up. Read: hold the ribbon at ~0.8 V as a suspended gate; the up/down gap changes gate coupling ~1.5x, which gives a ~10^3 channel-current ratio while the read force is only 18% of the snap force (non-destructive). Cells sit in BEOL tiers above CMOS periphery. Because the state is mechanical, retention is set by a ~45-80 kT elastic barrier, not by leakage.
why: Refresh energy and standby power go to zero (non-volatile); intrinsic write energy is ~2-4 aJ, versus ~3 fJ stored on a 1-beta cell plus ~46 fJ per refresh; mechanical switching is sub-ns (f0 = 2-15 GHz). Density reaches 1-beta parity only with two BEOL tiers of 50 nm ribbons. The step change is on energy and volatility, not density.

title: Hf-free MPB zirconia with work-function-biased operating point
idea: Today's DRAM uses Al-doped ZrO2 (k ~40, EOT ~0.6-0.7 nm). The highest reported hafnia-zirconia k values (56-64) sit at the morphotropic phase boundary (MPB) between ferroelectric-orthorhombic and tetragonal phases, using HZO superlattices that contain Hf. Here the stack is Zr-only ZrO2 (5.5-6 nm) whose phase balance is set by dopant (Al, Si, Y), thickness and electrode strain. An antiferroelectric-like ZrO2 has its highest small-signal permittivity near its field-induced transition; a built-in bias from work-function-asymmetric electrodes (TiN bottom, doped-SnO2 or MoO2 top) shifts that peak into the 0-0.5 V storage window. The capacitor is otherwise a standard pillar or stub.
why: EOT 0.55 -> ~0.41 nm (k 40 -> 56): the same 5.4 fF from a 0.97 um pillar instead of 1.29 um (AR 62 -> 46), or +34% Cs at the same height, Hf-free. A modest step on its own; it compounds with B2-01 (taller AAO cups) or B2-08 (shorter bitlines).

title: H-free sputtered-Si laser grains as in-stack CMOS and floating-body tiers
idea: Sputter amorphous Si at ~100 C (no PECVD hydrogen) over ~0.5-1 um of SiO2 that carries a lattice of small grain-filter holes, then melt it with an excimer-laser pulse: the mu-Czochralski process grows one location-controlled single-crystal grain (3-7.5 um) from each hole, with electron/hole mobilities of 460-510 / 121-250 cm2/Vs reported by the Delft group. The ~100 ns pulse heats only the top ~0.3 um, so oxide tiers below stay cool. Use the grains for (a) complementary sense amps and decoders inside the stack, without Smart Cut's hydrogen implant (B3-09's main risk), and (b) floating-body capacitor-less 1T cells, which need holes and therefore cannot be made in n-type IGZO, for Ge-free 3D silicon DRAM tiers.
why: In-stack p-FET drive 8-17x that of a p-type oxide TFT with zero implanted hydrogen; Ge-free, epi-free floating-body tiers (1-beta parity at ~17 tiers, 1 bit).

title: Seconds-ULTRARAM: a resonant-tunnelling floating gate retuned from 1,000-year retention to DRAM-class speed
idea: A floating gate above a III-V (or 2D) channel is isolated by a triple-barrier resonant-tunnelling stack. Two quantum wells of different thickness sit between three barriers and line up only at the programming bias (~2.5 V today), so electrons pass resonantly with no hot-carrier damage; off resonance the stack blocks. The read is a non-destructive channel-conductance measurement, making this a gain cell with no capacitor. The DRAM retune thins the barriers and wells, which lowers the retention target from 1,000 years to seconds or days, pulls the resonance voltage toward ~1-1.5 V and raises current density for ns writes. A 2D van der Waals version (graphene/hBN/MoS2 resonant barriers) could be transferred onto Si BEOL.
why: Refresh energy falls 1e3-1e6x (1 s to 1 day retention); writes cost ~1e-17-1e-16 J, against fJ-class DRAM cells plus periphery; crystalline barriers make 1e15-cycle endurance plausible.

title: Sliding-ferroelectric 2D gain channel (fatigue-free polarization)
idea: In AB/BA-stacked bilayers, an out-of-plane polarization flips when one layer slides by a fraction of a lattice constant. No ions move, so there is no oxygen-vacancy migration and no charged-defect build-up. A semiconducting 3R-MoS2 bilayer can serve as both channel and ferroelectric, or a bilayer-hBN gate ferroelectric can sit on a MoS2/IGZO channel. Polarization ~0.7 uC/cm2 (~4e12 e/cm2) shifts Vt by 0.16-0.30 V per state at EOT 0.8-1.5 nm, a 0.3-0.6 V window. The cell is non-volatile with a non-destructive gain read, written at <1 V in ns.
why: [SPECULATIVE at array scale] A ferroelectric 1T DRAM-class cell with endurance on a path to >=1e12-1e15 (1e11 shown), zero refresh, and sub-1 V ns writes: closes the 1e8x endurance gap that kills hafnia FeFETs.

title: Photonic periphery wafer: every bonded DRAM die is born with optical I/O
idea: Samsung's 4F2 DRAM builds the periphery on a separate wafer bonded under the cells. Make that periphery wafer in a monolithic photonics-CMOS process (microring modulators, Ge photodetectors, waveguides and 45 nm-class transistors on one wafer) so every DRAM die has optical I/O built in. The memory die connects to compute over fibers or a photonic interposer at metre scale, so capacity is not limited by the 8-12 HBM stacks that fit around a GPU or by TSV stacks. Closed-loop heaters keep the rings locked as DRAM die temperature moves.
why: DRAM at a distance at ~3.4 pJ/bit (HBM parity) instead of ~10-20 pJ/bit for off-package DDR [UNVERIFIED], ~500 GB/s per die, and unlimited capacity per accelerator; no TSVs or HBM stacking on the memory side. Energy is NOT better than HBM today.

title: Coolant-backed memory wafer: microchannels in the memory layer of a memory-on-logic stack
idea: In a face-to-face memory-on-logic stack (B3-02, or any bonded DRAM-over-logic), etch 100-200 um deep microchannels into the back of the thick memory wafer, away from its devices, and run warm water through them. The memory devices then sit only ~50 um of silicon plus their own BEOL from the coolant, while the logic's heat crosses the memory on its way out. With in-silicon microchannels of the kind Microsoft and Corintis demonstrated in 2025, the memory layer runs ~9-28 K above coolant instead of at the 70-105 C of a cold-plate GPU junction. DRAM retention roughly doubles for every 10 C drop, so a Si 1T1C array at ~45 C holds a 64 ms tail cell for ~1 s.
why: Refresh energy and refresh busy-time 8-16x lower for ordinary Si DRAM (64 ms -> 0.5-1 s; 7.6% -> 0.5-0.9% of time), and standard DRAM becomes viable directly on 1 kW logic without switching to oxide cells.

title: Graceful-forgetting KV memory: leakage as the eviction policy [SPECULATIVE]
idea: KV elements are stored sign-separated: the sign sits in exact rows, the magnitude as a 4- or 8-level charge in true-cell polarity, so leakage only ever reduces magnitude. Rows holding the recent window, attention-sink tokens and controller-flagged heavy hitters are refreshed under a lease (B4-03). All other KV rows are never refreshed. Over seconds to minutes their magnitudes droop level by level. A fully discharged row reads as all zeros, and the allocator reclaims it on zero-detect. The model sees a continuous 'forgetting curve' resembling H2O/StreamingLLM-style eviction, at zero refresh energy. Training or fine-tuning with the decay model (as RANA did for CNNs) teaches the network to expect it.
why: [SPECULATIVE] KV refresh energy -> 0 outside the leased window, with automatic capacity reclamation. Long-context KV footprint is bounded by the forgetting time constant rather than by context length.

title: In-tier complementary-oxide sense amplifiers (no-bond short bitlines)
idea: Build complementary oxide TFT latch sense amplifiers (n-IGZO/ZTO + p-TeSeOx, mobility ~15 cm2/Vs, on/off 1e6-1e7) in a dedicated BEOL tier above or below the memory tier(s), connected by short vias to 64-cell local bitline segments. Short bitlines (Cbl ~8 fF instead of ~35 fF) cut the needed storage capacitance to ~1.2 fF and allow VARY ~0.4 V; the local SA restores the cell and drives a global bitline to the Si periphery. In 3D stacks one SA tier serves N memory tiers, so bitline capacitance no longer grows with tier count. Offset-cancelled (auto-zero) SA topology absorbs oxide Vt mismatch.
why: ~27x lower bitline CV2/2 energy per sense (17.5 -> 0.64 fJ) and ~4.5x lower Cs requirement (5.4 -> ~1.2 fF), monolithically, without a second bonded wafer.

title: Quantum-dot charge RAM at 4 K: spin-qubit process lines repurposed for dense cryogenic memory
idea: On a 300 mm Si/SiGe or Si-MOS spin-qubit process, each cell is a gate-defined dot (plunger gate) with a barrier gate to a shared reservoir lead. A bit is 'full' (~10-30 electrons) or 'empty'; Coulomb blockade is not needed, only the barrier. Write: open the barrier (ns tunnelling) with the plunger set. Hold: the barrier is pinched off, so tunnel rates are far below 1e-6/s and thermal activation over ~50 meV (~140 kT) is impossible at 4 K. Read: a single-electron-transistor charge sensor shared by 4-8 dots, or gate reflectometry, with crossbar-shared gate lines. Cryo-CMOS drives the lines.
why: 0.05-0.1 Gb/mm2 (0.11-0.23x DDR5) at 4 K, ~2,000-4,000x denser than superconducting memory arrays; gate writes of 25-400 zJ (12-200 aJ at the wall); no refresh.

title: DNA-brick nanotrench templates for an EUV-free cell lattice
idea: On a wafer with coarse lithographic landing pads (ArF, ~80-100 nm), DNA-brick crystals assemble into nanotrench arrays whose pitch is programmable (10-40 nm) and whose registry is set by the pads. The DNA is mineralised (silicification or metal infiltration, as in sequential infiltration synthesis) or used directly as an etch mask, and the pattern transfers into a hardmask for the capacitor or channel holes, or for the bitline and wordline lines. Only the array layers use DNA; the periphery uses conventional lithography or sits on a bonded wafer. Because DNA is molecularly addressable, a single template can also carry non-periodic features such as pads and cuts.
why: Replace up to 5-7 EUV exposures ($825-1,155 per wafer at 1c, per A1) with ~$0.5-25 of DNA per wafer and room-temperature aqueous assembly; pitch headroom is 3.4x finer than today's 35 nm capacitor pitch.

title: Redox-molecule pseudocapacitor with natural multi-level plateaus (ZettaCore revival)
idea: ZettaCore's cell is a standard DRAM 1T cell whose capacitor is replaced by a porphyrin self-assembled monolayer between electrodes, an electrochemical cell. Charge is held in the molecules' discrete redox states, which appear at fixed potentials (e.g., +0.5 and +0.8 V), so voltage levels quantize naturally: multi-level storage without analog trimming. Retention of minutes was reported, vs tens of ms for DRAM. The twist: tether the SAM to a TiN pillar wall, fill the gap with an ALD-compatible solid ion conductor (or confined ionic liquid) for counter-charge, and read through an IGZO access device with 3-level sensing.
why: 2.4-4.9x signal charge per area -> pillar 1,300 -> 270-540 nm at equal charge per state; 1.6-2 bits/cell from discrete plateaus -> up to ~2x density at the same cell.

title: Coil-stacked HBM: inductive links instead of TSVs, NAND-style wire-bonded power
idea: Replace HBM's through-silicon vias and micro-bumps with inductive-coupling links: each thinned DRAM die carries ~2,000 small coils in its top metal over the array, and data hop vertically between dies by magnetic coupling (Keio's ThruChip Interface). Power enters the way NAND stacks do it: staggered dies with wire bonds, or a few coarse power vias at the die edge. The DRAM die loses its TSV keep-out field and the stack loses TSV/bump yield loss; coils also tolerate several um of misalignment, so stacking needs no fine-pitch alignment.
why: HBM wafer-per-bit tax 3x -> ~2.0-2.3x (+28-50% HBM bits per wafer) with no hybrid-bonding dependence. Energy is NOT improved: ~0.7 pJ/bit per coil hop vs ~0.15 pJ/bit per TSV layer.

title: Compression-funded ECC: compressible rows earn slow refresh for free
idea: On write, the controller compresses each line: exponent Huffman for float tensors, base-delta-immediate or zero-run for integers and pointers. If the result is <=54 B, it appends 70 parity bits (t=7 BCH over GF(2^10)) in the same 64 B slot and sets a mode bit in the existing ECC/metadata side-band. A per-row counter tracks whether every line in the row is in 'strong' mode; strong rows move to a slow refresh bin (RAIDR-style Bloom filter) and weak rows stay at 64 ms. A line that becomes incompressible demotes its row immediately, the safe direction. Reads run the full decode only when the cheap syndrome is nonzero.
why: 8-16x lower refresh energy (0.5-1 s interval) on fully compressible rows at zero capacity overhead. Float tensors compress to ~44 B per line, so this covers most of an AI accelerator's DRAM.

title: Origami memory stack: one thin membrane folded into N layers, wired through the folds [SPECULATIVE]
idea: Build N memory die images side by side as one continuous thin membrane (an oxide-cell array plus 3-4 metal levels, ~1.5-3 um thick) on a glass carrier with a laser-release layer, wiring neighbouring dies together across the gaps with ordinary BEOL lines. Release the membrane and fold it accordion-style into an N-layer stack bonded with thin adhesive, with fold radii of ~150-300 um. Vertical connectivity is the BEOL wiring that runs continuously around each fold, so there are no TSVs, no micro-bumps and no die-to-die alignment. The folded stack lands on a logic base die like HBM.
why: [SPECULATIVE] HBM-like stacks at near-planar wafer cost per bit: stacking tax 3x -> ~1.05-1.1x (fold loss 4.5-8.6%), with 20,000+ vertical wires per fold.

title: ECC-paid capacitor: let the code, not the capacitor, carry the last 4 sigma
idea: Today's ~50 mV sense budget exists so that every one of ~1.7e10 cells reads correctly at ~7 sigma of sense-amp (SA) offset and coupling noise, with only on-die SEC as backup. Re-centre the array on a raw BER target of 1e-4 per read. A t=8 BCH code (80 check bits per 512 data bits) in the memory controller or HBM/CXL logic base die absorbs the errors; optionally the SA fires two extra comparator thresholds to hand one soft-information bit per cell to a NAND-style soft decoder. With dV_min of 26 mV instead of 50 mV, the ZrO2/TiN pillar storage node can hold ~2.7 fF instead of 5.4 fF on the same 512-cell bitline: ~640 nm tall instead of 1,300 nm. An SA's offset is static, so codewords run along the row (each bit through a different SA), and outlier SAs are fused out at test like today's column repair. The same rule gives a 0.6 fF cell on a 64-cell local bitline in a 3D tier.
why: Capacitor height 2.0x lower (1,300 -> ~640 nm, aspect ratio 62 -> 30) at a 1e-4 raw BER, or 2.5x lower (-> ~525 nm, AR 25) at 1e-3, for +9 to +21 points of check bits (15.6-27.3% vs DDR5's 6.25%). 3D or local-bitline tiers need only 0.5-0.6 fF instead of 1.2 fF.

title: Tensor-aware codec in the memory controller (hardware DFloat11 + optional lossy KV)
idea: A codec in each GPU memory partition, with a matching engine in the HBM4 logic base die for capacity management, Huffman-codes the 8-bit exponents of tagged BF16 tensors. About 40 symbols are used, ~2.6 b entropy. Sign and mantissa are packed raw, 32 values per 64 B sector -> ~44 B. Fixed-rate block coding (32 exponents in a 96-112 b budget with an escape code) keeps random access at sector granularity. An optional lossy mode, under software control, applies KIVI-style per-channel K / per-token V 2-bit quantisation with a full-precision residual window. Unlike LZ-class CXL compressors (Marvell Structera, ZeroPoint: 2-3x on general data), this codec targets floating-point tensors, which LZ compresses poorly.
why: Lossless x1.47 effective capacity and bandwidth for BF16 weights and activations, saving ~17.8 pJ of interface energy per value for ~0.2-0.5 pJ of decode. The lossy KV mode gives up to 2.6x peak memory.

title: Erasure-coded memory stacks: 16+2 dies, any two may fail
idea: Treat the dies of an HBM-class (or 3D wafer-bonded) stack like disks in RAID-6. Data channels are striped across dies with rotating parity computed in the logic base die. When a die fails (at stack test or in the field), the base die reconstructs its channels from the others in degraded mode, or remaps them to a spare die (simpler, preferred at test). Signal paths crossing a failed bond are protected by redundant TSV/bond pads with per-layer bypass, or by contactless inductive-coupling links, so one die's failure does not sever the chain. Power gets per-layer isolation switches. This lets stacks use non-known-good dies and imperfect bonds.
why: At 95% per-die-in-stack yield, 16-high stack yield rises from 44% to 94% with 16+2: 1.9x fewer dies per good stack-bit. At 90% yield the gain is 3.5x; at 98%, 1.2x.

title: Scrub-as-refresh: 1-second refresh, page-level code, lazy scrub
idea: Each 1 KB DRAM page gets ~2% spare columns holding a BCH code (t=12 over GF(2^14)). The refresh engine restores rows about every second with a plain activate-precharge; the array itself is unchanged. A background scrubber decodes and rewrites each row about once a minute, so errors from weak and VRT cells can accumulate for at most one scrub period. Decoding at every refresh would eat most of the savings, so the scrub is lazy. Three add-ons stretch the interval further. (a) Per-subarray canary rows with undersized caps set the interval from measured leakage at the actual temperature, not from the 85 C 6.4-sigma worst case. (b) Retention errors only go one way (charged -> discharged, polarity known per true/anti cell), so an asymmetric (Z-channel) code needs fewer parity bits. (c) A write encoder flips 64-bit words to minimise how many cells sit charged. Fast-path reads use the existing on-die SEC; the page code is consulted only when an error is detected.
why: ~15x less refresh energy, scrub included. Refresh busy time drops from 7.6% to 0.5% at 16 Gb, or from 20.5% to 1.3% at 64 Gb. All on today's Si 1T1C cell, for ~2% parity.

title: IGZO gated-diode strip: a capacitor-module-free 3D DRAM tier ('two-gate NAND-like DRAM')
idea: Each tier holds a horizontal GAA IGZO (or IGO) strip with two gates: an access wordline and a plate gate. Write '1': with the wordline on and the bitline at 0 V, electrons accumulate under the positively biased plate. Write '0': with the bitline high, the well stays empty. Read: precharge the bitline, open the wordline, pull the plate low, and the stored electrons transfer completely to the bitline. A '0' moves almost nothing because a fully depleted 10 nm IGZO film has near-zero depletion capacitance. The plate is a row-shared line driven at 2.5 V, so the signal is set by the plate swing, not VARY, and the bitline can run at ~0.45 V. Built like Kioxia's SiN-replacement horizontal IGZO tiers: both gates are word-plane metal, and no lateral recess-and-fill capacitor module is needed.
why: Removes the 3D capacitor module entirely. Per-tier footprint 0.011-0.016 um2 vs A1 base 0.030 um2 -> 3D density break-even falls from ~26 tiers to ~9-14 tiers. Array energy per access ~5 fJ vs ~38 fJ bitline CV2 today.

title: Shared-rail SOT tier on hot logic (4 MTJs per write rail)
idea: A W/Ta (or field-free FM/Ta) spin-orbit rail carries the write current; four MTJs sit on it, selected by per-MTJ voltage biasing (VCMA-assisted) or by staggered critical currents along the track. One write transistor and per-MTJ read selects are shared. Thermal stability is designed for 125 C junction temperatures, so data persist where Si DRAM would need ~4 ms refresh. Reads use TMR; writes take <10 ns at <100 fJ. This is not a commodity-density play; it attacks the memory-on-logic bottleneck.
why: 2.2-2.6x SRAM macro density (0.086-0.10 Gb/mm2 vs ~0.04) with zero standby/refresh at 125 C and >1e15 cycles; 0.19-0.23x 1b density (honest: it does not beat DRAM density).

title: Mirror-VCT: 4F2 oxide cells above and below one shared bitline plane (2F2 effective)
idea: Build a 4F2 vertical-channel 1T1C array (deposited IGZO/IGO pillars, ring wordlines) over a buried bitline plane, with capacitors on top, as in Samsung's VCT. Bond that face to the periphery wafer (the periphery-under-cell flow already flips the cell wafer), remove the handle down to the back of the bitline plane, and build a mirror-image 4F2 VCT array plus capacitors from the backside at <=400 C. Each bitline now connects cells above and below it, so one bitline layer, one set of bitline contacts and one periphery wafer serve two cell layers: 2F2 effective per bit. The backside module is all-deposited (ALD oxide channel, ALD ZrO2 MIM), so it never exceeds BEOL temperatures.
why: 2x density over single-sided 4F2: 0.88 Gb/mm2 (1.96x 1-beta) at F = 20 nm with DUV multipatterning only, or 1.62 Gb/mm2 (3.6x) at F = 14.7 nm; ~1.4-1.5x bits/$ vs single-sided VCT.

title: Panel-level 3D oxide memory [SPECULATIVE]
idea: Deposit 64-128 tier stacks on 620x750 mm glass using display-industry PECVD and sputter tools; pattern channel holes by step-and-repeat nanoimprint at ~100 nm features (large-area imprint is proven at 100-200 nm pitch for wire-grid polarizers); one HAR etch per tier group; spatial-ALD oxide channels. Each tile (a few mm) is self-contained, with complementary-oxide local sensing (B2-08), so there is no cross-panel overlay requirement; tiles are diced and bonded to small Si I/O chiplets. This revives ram-venture A1-03 (display-glass memory, killed at 2 um rules) by getting density from tiers rather than pitch.
why: F=100 nm, 3 b x 64 tiers -> 0.96 Gb/mm2 (2.1x 1-beta) on 6.6x the substrate area -> ~45 TB per panel; capital from display-class tools.

title: Deep-level charge bit: QD-Flash physics shrunk toward an atom-placed single-defect cell
idea: Ensemble version (exists): self-assembled GaSb or InGaSb quantum dots in a GaP matrix give ~1 eV hole localisation. A gate bias floods the dots with holes (capture, ns), and a reverse field empties them by field-assisted emission (350 ns measured, ~10 ns predicted). The stored charge sits above a channel whose conductance is read non-destructively. Single-defect version (2040 tools): hydrogen-depassivation lithography or deterministic single-ion implantation places 1-3 deep-level dopants or engineered defects in a crystalline barrier under a 10-15 nm gate. Each trapped charge is a quantised threshold step, so the cell is natively multi-level (bits = number of charges). No amorphous tunnel oxide sits in the write path, so there is no oxide wear.
why: [SPECULATIVE] 2.7-5x density (4F2 at F = 10 nm, 1-2 bits/cell), ~3.5 aJ gate write energy, and a refresh interval anywhere from 1 s to 1 day by picking a 1.0-1.3 eV level.

title: Capacitive-NDRO ferroelectric gain cell for a read-mostly DRAM tier
idea: An HZO (or Zr-rich) capacitor with asymmetric electrodes has a zero-bias capacitance that differs between its two polarization states (imec reports a capacitive window ~8.7 at 0 V). The capacitor is the coupling element of a read transistor gate (1T-1C_FE or 2T-nC with n<=4). A small read pulse (below coercive) on its plate couples more or less charge onto the gate, and the read transistor converts that to current. Reads are non-destructive and never switch polarization; writes are full switching pulses. The memory is non-volatile, so there is no refresh and no restore, and pages need not be activated wholesale. Small n is essential: capacitive coupling dilutes as 1/n.
why: Refresh -> 0 and restore -> 0 for read-mostly data. Read endurance >1e11 (shown) vs ~1e7 write; read energy ~CV2 of a ~1.5 fF node (~0.1-0.4 fJ) instead of a 10 KB page restore (~5.9 pJ per useful bit random).

title: Trailing-node fab reuse: CMOS-under-array deep-tier MLC oxide memory at F=65 nm
idea: Run the fab's 65 nm CMOS flow to build sense amps, decoders and write-verify DACs, then stack 16-24 tiers of vertical IGZO/ZTO 2T0C cells over them (CMOS-under-array, as in 3D NAND CuA), with one hole etch per tier group at F=65 nm, ALD channels and recessed gates. Each cell stores 3-4 bits by write-verify; long oxide retention gives the level stability that MLC needs. No bonding, no immersion, no EUV.
why: 1.8-2.7x 1-beta density and 1.7-3.5x 1-beta bits per wafer-dollar (before yield) at F=65 nm, in existing depreciated fabs with no new litho tools.

title: BEOL bonus tiers: oxide gain-cell tiers stacked on a finished Si DRAM die
idea: Take a conventional 1-beta-class DRAM die, give ~15% of its area to extra sense and write-verify circuits, and after its last metal and hydrogen alloy anneal, seal it with an Al2O3/SiN hydrogen barrier and deposit 8 tiers of oxide gain cells (coax 4F2 B3-04, or vertical 2T0C) over the whole die, periphery included. The fast Si 1T1C array remains the hot tier (~15 ns), and the oxide tiers above form a dense, low-refresh warm tier (~30-50 ns) in the same package and interface. The add-on is a BEOL module that a separate, cheaper fab could run on finished DRAM wafers.
why: Bits per die 1.4-4.8x with no new front end: conservative (10F2, 1 bit x 8) 22.9 Gb on a 16 Gb die area; coax 1 bit 45.5 Gb (2.85x); coax 2 bit 77.5 Gb (4.8x); bits/$ 0.7-4.0x depending on $100-475 per tier.

title: Procedural weights: seeds plus coefficients, regenerated in the memory path
idea: Each block of ~8 weights is approximated as a linear combination of 3-4 pseudo-random basis vectors. An LFSR generates them from a 16-bit seed, weighted by 4-bit coefficients (SeedLM-style). Only seeds and coefficients (~3-4 b/weight) are stored in DRAM. A generator array in the GPU memory partition (or the HBM base die) expands them to BF16/FP8 on the way to the tensor cores. The LFSR and MACs cost ~0.3 pJ per weight, against ~14-56 pJ to fetch 4-16 bits over HBM.
why: 4-5.3x fewer stored bits than BF16, but only 1.0-1.33x vs FP4. The step is real only if accuracy at ~3 b/weight beats plain FP4/INT3 quantisation.

title: NIL-only periodic cell wafer (bonded periphery makes every layer imprintable)
idea: A master template (e-beam- or DSA-written) is replicated into working templates; jet-and-flash imprint defines each field's hole or line lattice with no projection optics. Because the cell wafer of a bonded 4F2 VCT or vertical gain-cell array needs only 2-3 overlay-critical layers (channel holes, wordline, contact) and later layers self-align, NIL's overlay and pattern-variety weaknesses matter less. 3D templates can define line + contact in a single imprint (dual-damascene style). Defects are absorbed by redundancy and ECC (B2-15).
why: No EUV and no SAQP spacer loops on array layers: 2-3 imprint layers replace ~4-6 EUV/SAQP-patterned layers [ESTIMATE], worth ~$330-500/wafer at EUV rates; litho tool capex per wafer start plausibly several-fold lower [UNVERIFIED-PK on tool price].

title: Photonic periphery wafer bonded under the DRAM cell array
idea: 4F^2 VCT and 3D DRAM programmes (Samsung 10a VCT, VS-DRAM, SK hynix VG) all wafer-bond the periphery to the cell array. Here that periphery wafer is a monolithic CMOS + silicon-photonics process: 45 nm-class SOI with microring modulators, Ge photodiodes and WDM filters. It carries the global periphery (command decode, SerDes, ECC and codecs from B4-01/07) plus 8-16-wavelength microring transceivers. Sense amps and local drivers stay on the cell wafer, bonded to the photonic wafer at 1-10 um pitch. Each die exits through 2-4 waveguides edge-coupled to fibre or a photonic interposer, with an external laser source. Memory can then sit 1-10 m away on cool sleds (B4-13) or in pools. For capacity tiers, HBM's silicon interposer and TSV I/O tax disappear.
why: ~2-3 pJ/bit at metre reach (vs HBM 3.4-3.5 pJ/bit at millimetre reach and DDR5 ~10-20 pJ/bit), using DDR-density dies at ~1x DDR5 wafer per bit instead of HBM's 3x.

title: Crystalline crested-barrier selector: transistor-less 1S1C crosspoint DRAM in stacked decks
idea: Each cell is a stub capacitor (~14 nm x 300 nm, k ~40, ~0.9 fF) in series with a layered tunnel barrier at a 4F2 crosspoint. Likharev's crested profile (a thin high-barrier centre with lower flanks), or VARIOT's low-k/high-k/low-k stack, makes current extremely field-sensitive. At hold and half-select (V/2 or less) the barrier is effectively thick and leakage is limited by direct tunnelling. At write voltage the bands bend below the crest and Fowler-Nordheim current flows. The barrier must be crystalline (hBN/graphene stacks, AlN/GaN epitaxy or epitaxial oxides), not amorphous ALD, because the full write charge passes through it on every cycle. Bitlines are 64 cells long with sense amps under the array, and decks stack like 3D XPoint.
why: Two decks at F = 20 nm give 1.34x 1-beta cell density; four decks give 2.7x, or 1.6x at F = 26 nm, which is reachable with SAQP and no EUV. No access-transistor GIDL tail.

title: Hydrogen-lean batch-furnace mold for oxide 3D DRAM
idea: NAND-style oxide 3D DRAM needs a 32-128-pair SiO2/SiN mold; single-wafer PECVD films carry ~3-25 at.% hydrogen, and hydrogen drives IGZO Vt drift (H-doping under PBTI, which imec cut ~30x with an H+O anneal). With the periphery on a separate bonded wafer, the cell wafer's mold can be made hot: deposit the alternating stack in a batch LPCVD furnace (100-150 wafers per load, ~4% H in LPCVD SiN, <1% in high-temperature oxide), then out-gas it at 800-900 C before any oxide channel is deposited (for example by Kioxia-style SiN->IGZO replacement). Add per-tier ALD Al2O3 hydrogen barriers around the replacement channels and finish with an O-rich anneal instead of forming gas.
why: Hydrogen reservoir next to each channel 4-8x smaller (PECVD SiN 4.8e16 -> LPCVD 1.1e16 H/cm2 per 30 nm tier, or 5.9e15 for oxide), relaxing the fraction allowed to reach the channel for a 20 mV (3-bit) budget from 3 ppm to 13-24 ppm; mold deposition at ~11 wafer-minutes per 64-pair stack.

title: Voltage-clocked skyrmion shift register: magnetic bubble memory revived with gate clocks instead of currents
idea: A chiral multilayer (Pt/Co/MgO type, with perpendicular anisotropy and strong DMI) is patterned into tracks 2F wide. Gates at 2F pitch on 1.5 nm MgO modulate interface anisotropy through VCMA. Two-phase clocks with a built-in ratchet (an asymmetric gate profile) create a moving energy minimum that carries each skyrmion one bit-length per clock, like charge packets in a CCD. A skyrmionic MTJ at the track end reads the bit (20-70% contrast reported), and a VCMA/SOT nucleator writes it. The state is non-volatile between shifts. With no lateral current there is no electromigration or Joule heating, and thousands of tracks share each clock line.
why: [SPECULATIVE] Refresh goes to zero; ~47 aJ per gate toggle; no capacitor or access transistor per bit. Density is 1.34x WORSE than 1-beta per layer at F = 13.4 nm (parity needs F ~11.6 nm or two layers). This is an energy and volatility play, not density.

title: 1T + 2 tunnel-diode latch: a refresh-free static cell at near-DRAM density
idea: The storage node of a 1T cell sits between two series NDR diodes (resonant tunnelling or interband Esaki) tied to the supply and ground rails. Their I-V curves cross at two stable points near the rails, so the node self-restores against leakage, with no refresh, no tRFC and a non-destructive read. Van der Wagt's III-V RTD/HFET gain cell proved the latch at ~50 nW/cell. The new part is BEOL-stackable, ultra-low-current-density NDR diodes stacked on the capacitor/storage contact in ~8F2. Candidates: oxide double-barrier (Al2O3/ZnO/Al2O3 quantum well) or MIIM diodes, Si/SiGe resonant interband tunnel diodes, or vdW graphene/hBN resonant tunnelling.
why: Refresh energy and refresh time -> 0 (7.6% availability at 16 Gb, ~20% at 64 Gb recovered). Static standby set by valley current: break-even with today's refresh power at J_valley ~0.23 A/cm2 (25 nm diodes).

title: Lithium-niobate-on-insulator conductive-domain-wall memory
idea: Thin-film LiNbO3 bonded on SiO2/Si (LNOI) is single-crystal. Applying a field across two in-plane electrodes inverts a nano-domain, creating a head-to-head charged wall that conducts (giant DW conductivity); removing it erases. A small read voltage senses wall current without moving the wall (NDRO, ~1e3 on/off). Embedded selectors give >1e6 selectivity for crosspoint arrays. Being a single crystal, LN has no grain boundaries or oxygen-vacancy-rich interlayers, the source of hafnia's wake-up/fatigue; its endurance under ns pulses is the open question.
why: Non-volatile NDRO 2-terminal cell at 0.4-1 V. Density is NOT the step: 0.2x 1b per layer at F = 40 nm, 0.79x with 4 bonded layers. The claim is endurance and energy (no refresh, no restore), still to be proven.

title: Approximate 4-level DRAM for low-order planes and 2-bit KV
idea: A 2-bit DAC-driven write driver writes one of four levels (0, 0.35, 0.70, 1.05 V). Reads use charge sharing followed by a 3-threshold successive sense, with extra reference levels from split reference bitlines as in the 1997 4-level 4 Gb DRAM. Gray coding makes an adjacent-level error a +/-1 LSB error of the 2-bit field. MLC rows hold only data classes that tolerate ~1e-3 level error: KIVI-style 2-bit KV (one element per cell), the low mantissa planes of BF16 (with B4-04), and MX/FP4 element codes whose shared scales stay protected. Exact data stay single-level. On short bitlines (128 cells, e.g., with sense amps under the array) the same scheme becomes exact.
why: 2x bits per cell for approximate data on the existing 1-beta array: KV capacity x2 vs single-level 2-bit storage, and BF16 with the B4-04 split x2.28 vs ECC'd BF16. At 128-cell bitlines the same circuit reaches exact-grade error rates (6.5e-15).

title: GRS-linked LPDDR 'HBM-lite' on an organic substrate
idea: Stacks of standard LPDDR5X/6 dies (wire-bonded or face-to-face pairs) sit on an organic package beside a small logic buffer die. The LPDDR dies talk to the buffer over ~1-2 mm unterminated traces. The buffer talks to the accelerator over ground-referenced signalling (GRS: single-ended, a charge-pump negative rail, forwarded clock) at 20-25 Gb/s per pin across 5-30 mm of organic substrate. There is no silicon interposer and no TSV in the DRAM. Ten to sixteen such packages around an accelerator give HBM-class aggregate bandwidth.
why: ~3x fewer DRAM wafers per bit than HBM at 2.7-3.4 pJ/bit (HBM3E: 3.44), with no silicon interposer.

title: Yield firewall: spare tiers per block plus pre-tested tier groups
idea: Build 64 + s tiers per block and fuse out up to s defective tiers per block through the tier decoder (B3-08 makes tier selection programmable), so one killer defect in one tier no longer kills a block. For very tall stacks, build tiers in groups of 8 on separate carriers, run parametric tests on each group (vertical-bitline continuity, leakage, Vt maps from built-in test structures), and stack only good groups by die-to-wafer hybrid bonding. That turns a multiplicative 64-tier yield into a sum of 8-tier yields plus bond yields.
why: Required per-block-tier killer-defect rate relaxed 2.5x (0.2% -> 0.5%) for 6% area overhead at 97.5% die yield; pre-tested groups lift 64-tier stack yield from 53% to ~97% at 0.99 per tier.

title: Jot-RAM: image-sensor pinned wells and correlated double sampling for few-electron multi-level memory
idea: Each cell is a vertical buried n-well in p-Si, ~40 nm wide and ~600 nm deep, holding ~450 electrons. A p+ sheath pins the well so surface and sidewall states stay filled and cannot generate dark current. A transfer gate empties the well into a floating diffusion shared by 8 cells, and a source follower drives the column. The read uses correlated double sampling: reset the floating diffusion and sample it, transfer the charge, sample again. The difference counts electrons and cancels both kTC noise and source-follower threshold mismatch, which is exactly what limits multi-level gain cells (A3 puts the margin at 62 mV for 3 bits). Writes meter a charge packet back through the transfer gate (fill-and-spill, as in CCDs), so levels are set by potential rather than by a leaky capacitor's history.
why: 4 bits/cell at roughly 1-beta area per bit (0.99-1.23x) with no capacitor. At or below 45 C, the 6-sigma-tail refresh interval is ~0.1-1 s and the median ~14-100 s, against 64 ms today. At 85 C, retention drops to DRAM-like levels (~3 ms tail for a 10-electron budget). So the win is multi-level sensing, plus refresh relief only for memory that runs cool.

title: Flat AlBN ferroelectric capacitor with non-destructive capacitive read
idea: Sputter 5-10 nm wurtzite Al1-xBxN (x 0.02-0.15) at <=400 C on a planar landing pad: 2Pr*A for a 40x40 nm pad is ~4 fC (~26,000 e-), more than today's 1.3 um pillar delivers. Reads must not switch the film, so the state is read capacitively: the imprinted polarization gives different small-signal C (or a piezo/flexo-induced charge) for up and down states, sensed through a 2T gain cell on an oxide channel, so only writes wear the ferroelectric. Data are non-volatile: no refresh. A gain-cell or SRAM write buffer in front absorbs write traffic.
why: Zero capacitor height and zero refresh energy; 1-4 fC per bit from a planar 20-40 nm pad; Sc- and Hf-free. Gated by an endurance gap of ~1e5-1e9x.

title: AFE-reservoir stub capacitor (Hf-free antiferroelectric ZrO2)
idea: Tetragonal ZrO2 films 5-7 nm thick show a pinched double hysteresis loop: above ~1-1.5 MV/cm they turn polar, below a lower field they snap back. Write '1' to ~1.3 V (polar state, storing induced polarization plus linear charge); write '0' to 0 V (never crosses the forward field). Precharge the bitline low (~0.35 V, below the backward switching voltage) instead of VARY/2, so a '1' dumps its polarization onto the bitline as the film relaxes while a '0' gives only linear charge. The backward branch is a near-constant-voltage plateau: leakage drains polarization before the node voltage droops, a built-in charge reservoir. Electrode work-function asymmetry (TiN/W or TiN/Mo) or fixed charge shifts the loop to tune the plateau voltage. Same ALD ZrO2/TiN tool set as today, applied to a much shorter pillar or a short horizontal capacitor in a 3D tier.
why: 3-6x signal charge per um2 of capacitor wall -> capacitor height 1,300 nm -> 210-420 nm (AR 62 -> 10-20) at equal signal; up to ~3x retention stretch from the plateau; horizontal 3D capacitor 3-6x shorter.

title: VCMA crosspoint MRAM with deliberately relaxed (refreshed) retention
idea: Each crosspoint is an OTS selector plus a perpendicular CoFeB/MgO MTJ with a high VCMA coefficient. A ~0.5-1 ns voltage pulse lowers the anisotropy so the free layer precesses half a turn, with no write current through a transistor, so there is no access transistor and the cell is 4F2. Thermal stability Delta is chosen for refreshed operation (Delta ~44-48 for 1 s to 1 min, vs ~64 for 10-year non-volatility), allowing a smaller or thinner free layer and lower write voltage. A 'refresh' is a TMR read plus conditional rewrite, done rarely. Four BEOL decks stack over CMOS.
why: 2.9x 1b density (4 decks, F = 20 nm) or 1.3x (F = 30 nm, no EUV); write energy 6-20 fJ vs a 46 fJ refresh plus pJ-class activation; refresh 15x+ less frequent than DRAM.

title: Carrier-is-memory: the mandatory carrier wafer of backside-power logic becomes a DRAM wafer
idea: In backside power delivery the finished front-side BEOL is flipped and bonded to a carrier wafer, the original substrate is ground away and power is wired in from the back, so the front-side signal wiring ends up facing the carrier. Replace that blank carrier with a full DRAM wafer (1-beta-class 1T1C or an oxide-cell wafer) whose die map matches the logic reticle, and make the bond a Cu-SiCN hybrid bond at 1-2 um pitch instead of a plain dielectric fusion bond. The memory die keeps its sense amps and bank logic but drops pads, PHYs and TSVs; commands, data and memory power cross the bond. The memory wafer stays thick and becomes the heat-spreading side of the stack (pair with B3-03). For a wafer-scale engine, the same move puts a whole 300 mm DRAM wafer (~3.9 TB) under the compute wafer.
why: Memory interface energy ~12x lower (3.5 -> ~0.28 pJ/bit), saving ~200-410 W per accelerator at 8-16 TB/s; 45-53 GB per 800 mm2 logic die with zero added footprint and no HBM stacking; ~$1.7-2.3/GB of added memory at DRAM-wafer cost.

title: Thin wafer-on-wafer DRAM with spare layers (64-high in today's package height)
idea: Stack whole DRAM wafers thinned to ~4-10 um wafer-on-wafer with bumpless via-last TSVs of ~1-2 um diameter, the Tokyo Tech / WOW Alliance (BBCube) approach. Because wafer stacking cannot select known-good dies, add spare layers (18 for 16, or 72 for 64) and let the base die map out failed die sites layer by layer after in-die repair. Thin silicon makes each TSV ~20x smaller in area including keep-out and cuts stack thermal resistance ~3x versus bump stacks, and 10 um layers allow 64-high stacks inside today's package height.
why: TSV+keep-out area ~21x smaller per TSV; 64-high stacks in 640 um (4x capacity per stack vs 16-high); stack yield 94-99% with 12.5% spare layers at >=95% die-site yield.

title: Maskless interference lithography for an all-periodic cell wafer
idea: Two (or four) coherent 193 nm beams interfere in water immersion to write a fringe pattern at half-pitch ~34.5-36 nm; two crossed exposures give post or hole lattices at ~70 nm pitch, and one SADP halves that to ~35 nm. Scanning-beam interference lithography (Doppler writing) phase-locks the fringe to wafer marks for overlay and covers 300 mm continuously. Array edges and the few non-periodic features are cut by a coarse KrF/i-line trim exposure whose overlay is not critical. Possible only because bonded periphery has removed all random logic from the cell wafer.
why: No masks and no EUV for array layers; 4F2 at F~17-18 nm with one SADP; litho tool capex estimated ~10x below an ArF immersion scanner and ~50-100x below EUV [ESTIMATE: no projection optics].

title: Ru-free rutile: SnO2-templated TiO2 short-stub capacitor
idea: Cap the TiN bottom electrode with 3-5 nm of ALD Ta-, Nb- or F-doped SnO2 (conductive, rutile/cassiterite structure, a=4.74 A vs rutile TiO2 a=4.59 A). ALD TiO2 (optionally lightly Al-doped to suppress leakage) nucleates epitaxially in the rutile phase on the SnO2 grains at 250-340 C, giving k ~60-100 without the >800 C anneal or the Ru/RuO2 template used in earlier rutile work. A doped-SnO2 top electrode makes the stack symmetric and keeps the high-work-function contact. At 7 nm physical thickness the EOT is 0.34-0.40 nm. The capacitor is used either to shorten the 1-beta pillar from 1.3 um to 0.8-0.95 um, or as a 0.30-0.35 um stub holding ~2 fF for short-bitline, 4F2 or 3D-tier cells.
why: 1.4-1.6x more capacitance per area than ZrO2-based stacks (EOT 0.40/0.34 vs 0.55 nm): equal Cs from a capacitor 27-38% shorter (AR ~39-45 instead of 62), or 2 fF from a 0.30-0.35 um stub; zero Ru and zero Hf.

title: Capacitor-first inverted flow with perovskite super-k
idea: On a bare carrier or Si wafer, deposit a conductive-oxide bottom electrode (LaNiO3, Nb:SrTiO3 or doped SnO2), sputter/ALD 10-12 nm (Ba,Sr)TiO3 or SrTiO3 into short pillars or cups, and RTA at 650-750 C to crystallize (k 100-250); add the top electrode and planarize. Then build vertical IGZO/ZTO access transistors directly on the capacitor top contacts at <=400 C (the OCTRAM-style transistor-over-capacitor arrangement), and finally hybrid-bond the logic periphery wafer on top. Because the capacitor comes first, no transistor, metal or gate stack ever sees the perovskite anneal. The bit is a normal 1T1C charge sensed through a short bitline.
why: 3-4x shorter capacitor at equal charge: k 150 (EOT 0.26 nm) gives 4.6 fF from a 0.5 um stub (vs 5.4 fF from 1.3 um today), AR ~23 instead of 60-75; a 0.3 um stub gives 1.8-3.8 fF, enough for 64-128-cell bitlines.

title: BitNet-native charge-sharing popcount PIM in commodity 1T1C
idea: Ternary weights {-1, 0, +1} are stored as two bit-masks (positive and negative) in 1T1C rows, and activations are bit-sliced (INT8 into 8 binary planes). For each activation plane, the controller first RowClones the selected weight rows, ANDed with the activation mask (Ambit-style), into dedicated compute rows. It then activates 8 compute rows at once on the same bitlines. Charge sharing gives a bitline voltage proportional to the number of charged cells (0-8), which a 3-bit flash ADC shared by 8-16 bitlines in the SA stripe digitises. A small near-bank adder shifts and accumulates the partial sums. Weights never leave the bank.
why: 12-35x lower energy per decode GEMV than reading ternary weights over HBM (0.39 J vs 0.011-0.033 J per token for a 70B ternary model), plus ~8x internal bandwidth.

title: HBF weight tier with read-disturb-aware 'weight mode'
idea: HBF stacks NAND dies on TSVs behind an HBM-like interface (OCP spec August 2026: 256 GB/die, 512 GB per 16-high stack, ~1.6 TB/s read). Weights are written once per deployment, while KV and activations stay in DRAM. Each decode step reads every weight page, so a page sees 1e5-3e6 reads per day. Read disturb (pass-voltage stress on the unselected wordlines of a block) then forces periodic reclaim, that is, a rewrite. The 'weight mode' has four parts: program weights in pSLC, or TLC with relaxed retention; interleave each tensor across many blocks so read counts stay even; track per-block read counters and relocate before the disturb limit; and keep a second replica on another die to alternate reads when the disturb budget is tight.
why: HBF claims 8-16x HBM capacity at similar cost. In endurance-safe pSLC weight mode it still gives ~3-5x HBM capacity per $, against HBM's ~3x DDR5 wafer cost per bit.

title: BEOL-only cell mini-line on reusable glass carriers, bonded to trailing-node periphery
idea: Oxide gain-cell or oxide 1T1C stacks (8-32 tiers) are deposited and patterned on a 300 mm CTE-matched glass carrier with a laser-release layer, using only PVD/ALD/PECVD, dry etch, ArF/NIL, CMP, cleans and a hybrid bonder: no >450 C furnaces, implanters, epitaxy or EUV. The finished stack is hybrid-bonded face-down to a periphery wafer (sense amps, decoders, I/O) from a trailing-node foundry at 1-2 um pitch, which A3's model says is enough for litho-light oxide pitches. The glass is laser-debonded through its transparent back and reused.
why: Cell-side capex ~$44-68k per wafer-start-per-month vs $145-170k for a DRAM greenfield (2.5-3.3x lower) [ASSUMPTION: BEOL-only tool set = 30-40%]; prime-Si demand of dual-wafer (periphery-under-cell) DRAM -45-49% by reusing the cell carrier 10-50x.

title: Altermagnetic tunnel-junction RAM: MRAM without stray fields
idea: The free layer is an altermagnet (RuO2, CrSb, MnTe or newer candidates) whose Neel vector sets spin-dependent tunnelling through an MgO-type barrier to a reference electrode. Writing uses spin-splitter or spin-orbit torque from an adjacent line, or the altermagnet's own current-induced torque; reading uses TMR. Zero net moment removes dipolar coupling to neighbours and to external fields, so crosspoint pitch can drop from ~2.5 to ~1.5 diameters, and exchange-enhanced switching could reach ps timescales. Endurance is magnetic, with no wear mechanism.
why: [SPECULATIVE] 2.8x denser than ferromagnetic MTJ crosspoints at the same diameter (900 vs 2,500 nm2 at d = 20 nm), ~1.2x 1-beta per deck; non-volatile; potential ps writes.

title: Vt-coded in-stack tier decoder: kill the staircase so 3D DRAM lines can be short
idea: 3D NAND reaches each tier's horizontal line through a staircase whose length grows with tier count; DRAM wants short lines (sub-page activation, low RC), and at 64 tiers a ~32 um staircase is longer than a 512-cell line. Instead, route every tier's horizontal line under 2*log2(N) vertical select-gate pillars before it merges into one common vertical contact. In each tier, each select region is permanently depletion-mode (always on) or enhancement-mode according to that tier's binary address, so driving the pillars with an address and its complement opens exactly one tier's path. The code is written per tier during deposition with one coarse (um-scale, i-line) block mask, or, as in Macronix-style LSM for 3D NAND, by programming charge-trap select gates once at test.
why: Line-termination area 12x smaller at 64 tiers (32 um staircase -> 2.7 um) and 21x at 128; line-end overhead for a 128-cell line 83% -> 30%, enabling 4x shorter wordlines and correspondingly less activation overfetch.

title: 1T-TaS2 charge-configuration memory: picosecond, attojoule switching for the 4 K tier
idea: Thin 1T-TaS2 flakes or films sit between two electrodes. A ps current pulse reorders the charge-density-wave domain configuration into a metastable 'hidden' metallic state (low resistance), and a longer, weaker pulse restores the insulating Mott-CDW state. The state is non-volatile at cryogenic temperature and is read resistively. Cells form a 4F2 crosspoint with selectors, or 1T1R with cryo-CMOS.
why: Write energy of ~24-94 aJ at 50-100 nm and ~2 ps (0.5 ps floor), ~100x below the superconducting nanowire memory's ~10 fJ cell energy; 0.67x 1-beta density per deck at F = 20 nm if the crosspoint works.

title: Direct-tunnel charge-trap '3D AND' DRAM built with 3D-NAND tools
idea: Vertical channel holes (poly-Si or ALD IGZO/IGO) with vertical source/drain lines pass through stacked word planes (3D AND/NOR topology, as in SunRise 3D NOR and Macronix-style 3D AND). Gate stack: ~1.5-2 nm bandgap-engineered SiO2/SiON tunnel layer, SiN trap layer and Al2O3 blocking layer. Low-field direct tunnelling (few V) avoids the hot-carrier and FN damage that limits NAND endurance; retention falls to seconds-minutes, which is the trade: quasi-volatile. Each cell is read individually with ns-class parallel sensing on short vertical bitlines; refresh is 16-1,500x less frequent than DRAM.
why: 2.7-7.2x 1b density at 64-256 tiers on a NAND-class (EUV-free) line; refresh energy and time 16x (1 s) to 1,562x (100 s) lower.

title: NbO2 Mott threshold switch as an in-stack local sense element
idea: A ~10-20 nm NbO2 device biased just below its threshold voltage sits on each local bitline segment. A '1' signal (~200 mV on a 64-cell segment) tips it over threshold; Joule heating drives the Mott transition (~1080 K locally) and the device snaps to a low-resistance state, producing a large current spike that a shared global sense line or latch detects. A '0' leaves it insulating. The device is a regenerative, abrupt, non-linear element only ~20 nm across, stackable in the cell tiers. Mott insulators cannot isolate a storage node (their off-state conductivity is many orders too high), so this card uses the transition only for sensing.
why: [SPECULATIVE] Enables 64-cell local bitlines inside a 3D/BEOL stack: Cs need drops 5.4 -> ~1.2 fF and VARY to ~0.4 V (array energy ~16x lower per A1), without 8x more silicon sense amps.

title: Myelinated bitline: vacuum-sheathed bitline segments with non-latching 2T 'nodes of Ranvier'
idea: Bitlines are enclosed laterally in a sealed vacuum or air cavity, extending today's air spacers to the full bitline sidewall and the bitline-to-landing-pad gap. Every 32-64 cells the bitline breaks at a 'node': a BEOL IGZO 2T amplifier (source follower plus reset, non-latching) stacked above the array. The node turns the local segment's charge-sharing voltage into a current on a global bitline, and the main sense amp sits at the end as it does today. Unlike a local sense amplifier, the node neither latches nor restores, so it fits in BEOL above the array; restore runs through the global path.
why: The Cs requirement falls from 3.65 to 0.6-0.8 fF (32-64-cell segments), so the capacitor is ~150-200 nm tall instead of ~1.3 um. The vacuum sheath alone lowers Cbl by only 1.5-1.7x.

title: Self-timed NEMS-selector crosspoint: a two-terminal hysteretic nanorelay that charges the capacitor and lets go by itself
idea: Each cell is a stub capacitor (~1 fF) plus a vertical or lateral 2D/ALD nanobeam relay (gap ~5 nm, stiffness ~1 N/m) at a 4F2 crosspoint. Relays have abrupt pull-in and release thresholds (effectively 0 mV/decade), so a half-select voltage below pull-in cannot close them. Write '1': the bitline at 2.2 V closes the relay; the capacitor charges until V_BL - V_cap drops below release (0.75 V); the relay opens and V_cap settles at ~1.45 V, set by mechanics rather than timing. Write '0': a slightly negative bitline leaves 0.45 V. Read: a bitline voltage between the two windows closes the relay only for '0' cells, producing a charge pulse (destructive, then restored). Hold: the gap is open vacuum, so leakage is through the capacitor dielectric only. Lines idle at mid-level and use V/3 biasing so unselected relays never see pull-in.
why: Retention of 6-58 s at 1 fF (against 64 ms); 2-4 decks of 4F2 give 1.3-2.7x 1-beta density at F = 20 nm; the stored level is set by mechanics.

title: Lifetime-leased refresh: streamed and dead data are never refreshed
idea: A lease table in the memory controller (or HBM base die) puts each 2 MB region in one of three classes. (i) 'Dead': freed pages, retired KV. (ii) 'Streamed with period <= P': weights and live KV in LLM decode, read every token. (iii) 'Normal'. Class (ii) rows are restored as a side effect of every full activation. A per-region activation timestamp certifies that each row was opened within tREF, and the controller issues a targeted refresh only for rows that miss the deadline. Class (i) rows get no refresh at all. For most of an inference HBM, the all-bank REF command and its tRFC blackout disappear. A further step is an HBM bin specified for 'access-guaranteed' use, with a relaxed retention screen. Dies that fail today's 32 ms retention test become usable for weights.
why: Refresh energy -> ~0 for streamed and dead regions, and 5-15% more usable HBM bandwidth in bandwidth-bound decode (x1.05-1.18 tokens/s), with no cell change. General servers with 30-50% dead memory get refresh energy x0.5-0.7.

title: TSV-free inductive stacking for short memory-on-logic stacks
idea: Dies thinned to ~10 um are glued rather than bump-bonded. Data crosses between stacked dies through pairs of ~30 um on-chip spiral coils at ~8 Gb/s each. Power and ground use a few highly doped silicon vias or edge connections. There is no TSV etch or fill, no microbump yield loss and no hybrid-bond overlay.
why: For 4-high stacks: no TSV or microbump process steps, ~26% less die area than TSVs (reported for a 7 nm SRAM stack), and ~2.7 pJ/b on the worst-case hop. For 16-high HBM it fails: 62-562 mm2 of coil per die, or 13.5 pJ/b through relays.

title: Nanogap (vacuum/air) tunnel-barrier floating node: flash-like retention without oxide wear
idea: The floating metal node (TiN or W, anchored on dielectric on one side) faces a write electrode across a 2.5-4 nm gap. The gap is made by removing an ALD sacrificial layer (carbon or Al2O3) and then sealed, like BEOL air-gaps or NASA's nanoscale vacuum-channel transistors, which work in air because the gap is far below the ~70 nm mean free path. The node is the gate of an IGZO or Si read transistor (2T-like gain cell), so the read is non-destructive. Writing uses field emission at a few V/nm (field enhancement 2-3 at edges); holding relies on the exponential non-linearity of tunnelling. Charge never passes through a solid dielectric, so there are no trap generation, SILC or charge-to-breakdown limits, the mechanisms that cap flash endurance at ~1e5. Low-work-function coatings (LaB6-class, 2.7 eV) cut write voltage, but even plain TiN (4.5 eV) works at 8 V.
why: [SPECULATIVE] A non-volatile, refresh-free DRAM-class gain cell: retention 3.7e4 s (2.5 nm gap, 2.7 eV) to >1e8 s (3 nm), writes in 0.4-40 ns. Endurance is not set by oxide damage, with a target of >=1e12.

title: Solid-state proton double-layer nano-capacitor [SPECULATIVE]
idea: Replace the high-k film with a 3-5 nm PECVD phosphosilicate-glass (PSG) proton conductor between ion-blocking TiN or W electrodes, optionally with a 1-2 nm pseudocapacitive WO3 or MnO2 skin. Applying the bit voltage (<=~1 V) moves protons a fraction of a nm to form double layers at both interfaces: an all-solid-state nano-supercapacitor with ~10-20 uF/cm2 (EDL) or ~100 uF/cm2 (pseudocapacitive) vs 6.3 uF/cm2 for EOT 0.55 nm. The access transistor and sensing are unchanged. MIT showed nanosecond proton shuttling through PSG at room temperature under ~1 V/nm fields.
why: 5.4 fF from a 0.41 um stub (EDL, 20 uF/cm2) or 0.08 um (pseudocapacitive, 100 uF/cm2) at 21 nm diameter, vs 1.3 um today: 3-16x shorter, with all-abundant P/Si/O/H/W.

title: DSA honeycomb: block-copolymer self-assembly for the capacitor/channel hole lattice
idea: Coat PS-b-PMMA (or a high-chi BCP for <30 nm) whose cylinder lattice period L0 (~28-40 nm) matches the 1-beta (35 nm) or 1c (32 nm) capacitor honeycomb. A single-exposure ArF immersion guide pattern (or chemical pre-pattern) at 2-3x the pitch registers the lattice and DSA multiplies density 3-4x, rectifying CD and placement noise. Sequential infiltration synthesis (TMA/H2O into PMMA) hardens the pattern into an AlOx mask for transfer into the mold (SiO2 or the carbon mold of B2-10). For 4F2 square lattices, chemo-epitaxy with a square guide is used.
why: Replaces 1-2 EUV or SAQP layers in the array: $165-330 per wafer (3.8-7.7% of a $4.3k 1c wafer) before netting DSA cost; the hole lattice comes from polymer physics rather than wavelength.

title: Thermal arbitrage: keep the bits away from the GPU's heat
idea: HBM sits millimetres from a ~1 kW GPU at 85-95 C (32 ms refresh above 85 C), and server DIMMs run 50-85 C. In a disaggregated design, capacity DRAM (KV pools, cold weights, CXL expanders) moves onto separately liquid-cooled sleds at 30-40 C, linked by optics (B4-14) or CXL. Refresh is set from on-die temperature and canary readings (B4-02), not the 85 C worst case. The cool margin can be spent three ways: (a) 4-30x longer refresh intervals; (b) multi-level rows (B4-05), whose droop budget is a third of single-level; (c) next-generation dies designed to a 'cool spec' with ~30% shorter capacitors.
why: Retention x3.7-18 from 85 C to 35 C (Arrhenius, Ea 0.25-0.55 eV; x32 by the 2x/10 C rule), so refresh energy and busy time fall 4-18x; or Cs 5.4 -> ~3.8 fF (the sense-limited floor), a ~30% shorter pillar.

title: Row-RAID: in-bank XOR parity rows built by triple-row activation
idea: For read-mostly regions (weights, and KV after it is written), the controller issues in-DRAM bulk-bitwise sequences that accumulate one parity row per group of 32 rows in a subarray. These are Ambit-style triple-row activation for AND/OR plus a dual-contact-cell NOT, composed into XOR. Group membership is interleaved so physically adjacent rows (the +/-1 and +/-2 victims of any aggressor) fall in different groups. Per-line ECC (on-die SEC or B4-01's BCH) detects a damaged row. The controller then XORs the other 31 rows and the parity inside the subarray and writes the reconstruction back. A write to a protected row updates parity with two in-DRAM XORs (old ^ new).
why: Row-hammer and weak-row tolerance for read-mostly data at ~3% capacity, instead of PRAC's <13% performance overhead today and up to 94% for future chips. Any single row per group may lose all its bits.

title: Broadcast weight bus: one copy of the model feeds N lock-stepped replicas
idea: A weight server (HBF or DRAM, as in B4-12/16) streams each layer's weights on a fixed schedule onto WDM optical waveguides, split 1:N by passive splitters (with semiconductor optical amplifiers if needed) to N accelerators. The replicas run decode in lock-step by layer, on a global layer clock. Each accelerator feeds the weight stream straight into its tensor cores through an SRAM skew buffer of a few MB, while its own HBM holds only KV and activations. One 4-16 TB/s stream serves all N receivers, because optical fan-out needs one modulation for any N.
why: Weights leave replica HBM: 22% (70B on 8x80 GB) to 72% (405B on 8x141 GB) of HBM is freed for KV. Per broadcast domain, N copies of the model become 1.

title: Grow-the-hole: bottom-up dual area-selective deposition replaces the high-aspect-ratio etch [SPECULATIVE]
idea: 3D memory molds are normally deposited and then plasma-etched with holes at aspect ratios of 40-80, the hardest and most fluorocarbon-hungry step in 3D NAND. Instead, define the hole lattice once at the bottom as metal seed dots and grow the stack around them. For each tier, selective CVD tungsten grows ~30 nm only on the exposed W pillar tops (selectivity holds for ~100 nm per cycle), a dielectric (SiO2 or SiN, alternating by tier) grows only on dielectric with a short-lived inhibitor on the W, and an in-situ NF3/H2 etch-back removes stray W nuclei. After the last tier the W pillars are dissolved, leaving vertical holes through the whole stack, aligned by construction.
why: [SPECULATIVE] Eliminates the high-aspect-ratio mold etch: AR 38 (64 tiers) to 77 (128 tiers) with zero plasma etch and no bow or twist; hole CD set by the seed, not by depth.

title: Cold-bond stack: room-temperature surface-activated hybrid bonding for oxide memory
idea: Standard hybrid bonding needs a post-bond anneal above ~350 C to close the Cu pads, and every sequential bond re-anneals everything below it. For oxide-channel memory wafers that cumulative heat (8-16 h at 350 C for an 8-layer stack) shifts Vt and redistributes hydrogen, which multi-level storage cannot tolerate. Use surface-activated bonding instead: Ar fast-atom-beam cleaning in ultra-high vacuum lets Cu-Cu (and, with Si nano-adhesion layers, dielectric) surfaces bond at room temperature without anneal. Memory layers can then be bonded after multi-level calibration and after hydrogen-sensitive steps, and heterogeneous layers (ferroelectric, photonic, organic) can join without a thermal limit.
why: Post-bond thermal budget 8-16 h at 350 C -> 0, removing a thermal dose equal to ~5-37 years at 85 C of activated drift kinetics per stack.

title: Capacitor-hole racetrack: electroplated domain-wall nanowires in DRAM's high-aspect-ratio mold
idea: Etch the standard honeycomb hole lattice (~20 nm diameter at 35-40 nm pitch) in oxide. Instead of conformal ALD electrodes, electroplate a magnetic nanowire up from a seed at the hole bottom, modulating composition (Co-rich/Ni-rich, or thin Cu spacers) every ~60 nm to make pinning notches. Bits are axial domains separated by Bloch-point domain walls, which cylindrical wires carry without the Walker breakdown that slows flat racetracks. A vertical select transistor under each hole (4F2/6F2 vertical-channel style) drives ~30 uA bipolar shift pulses through the wire. A 20 nm MTJ on the planarised top reads the top bit and writes it (STT, or SOT from a top heavy-metal line). Half of each track is shift buffer, giving 10 data bits per 1.3 um hole and 25 per 3 um hole.
why: ~10x (1.3 um holes) to ~25x (3 um holes) bits per 1-beta cell footprint: 4.5-11 Gb/mm2 in principle, or 1-beta density at ~3x larger F with no EUV. Refresh energy goes to zero.

title: Gallium-free, indium-lean oxide channels (ZTO / SnO2 / ITZO) for gain cells and VCT
idea: Deposit amorphous Zn-Sn-O (ZTO), SnO2, or In-lean In-Sn-Zn-O / In-W-O channels by ALD (or PVD for planar) at <=350 C, with the gate insulator and channel grown in one ALD chamber without a vacuum break (UMich) and Al2O3/SiO2 passivation (Hf-free, unlike the HfO2 used for the SJTU record). Cells are the same 2T0C/3T0C gain cells or 4F2 VCT access transistors now built with IGZO. Zn and Sn suppress oxygen-vacancy carriers less strongly than Ga, so thin (3-5 nm) channels, Al or Si doping, and O3 anneals set the threshold voltage. The bit is stored on the read transistor's gate (gain cell) or on a capacitor (VCT).
why: 100% Ga-free (and In-free for ZTO) oxide DRAM supply chain at >=1500 s demonstrated retention (~23,000x a 64 ms refresh interval), with 2-6 ns single-bit read on a 64-cell read bitline.

title: 77 K oxide MLC gain-cell stage for cryogenic and superconducting computers
idea: IGZO/IWO 2T0C gain cells (no capacitor) sit in BEOL tiers on a 77 K cryo-CMOS periphery wafer. At 77 K, oxide-cell leakage collapses (8,000 s reported for IGZO 2T0C) and threshold drift (PBTI, hydrogen motion) is thermally frozen. Si subthreshold swing falls to ~15-20 mV/decade, so periphery and wordlines run at ~0.4 / 1.0 V, and Cu resistance drops several-fold. Together these make 3-4 bits/cell with write-verify realistic. The stage links to 4 K superconducting logic through the thermal-break link in imec's architecture.
why: Array energy x0.13 (0.78 vs 5.9 pJ per useful bit); refresh cut ~1e5x; 3-4 bits/cell gives 1.2-1.6x 1-beta density per tier, ~17,000x the density of the best 4 K superconducting memory array.

title: Temperature-hardened negative-capacitance stub (FE/DE superlattice)
idea: A ferroelectric biased in the unstable middle of its Landau double well has negative differential capacitance C_FE < 0. In series with a dielectric (C_DE) and with |C_FE| > C_DE, the total capacitance C_DE/(1 - r) exceeds C_DE, where r = C_DE/|C_FE|. The stack is an ALD superlattice of Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 (or Zr-rich HZO) with ZrO2/Al2O3 layers on TiN, deposited in the same pillar or short horizontal capacitor. The twist is designing r against temperature: |C_FE| follows Curie-Weiss behaviour, so r is set to ~0.85 at the cold corner and falls to ~0.6 at 125 C. The capacitor then never crosses into hysteresis and still gives >=2.5x at the hot corner.
why: 2.5x (125 C) to 4.7x (25 C) capacitance per area -> pillar 1,300 -> ~430-650 nm for equal Cs; or the same height with a ~2.5-4x bigger signal at 1c/1d cell sizes.

title: Protonic gain cell (H+ in WO3 behind a PSG electrolyte)
idea: Three terminals: a WO3 channel between source and drain; a nanoporous PSG electrolyte (2-5 nm) above it; a Pd (or PdHx) gate that serves as the proton reservoir. A gate pulse at ~1 V/nm drives H+ into or out of WO3 in ns; each inserted proton is charge-compensated by an electron, which raises channel conductance. At read voltages the field is too low to move protons, so the state is non-volatile and the read is non-destructive. Multi-level storage is natural (analog conductance). The 'protonic nano-supercapacitor stub' variant, which uses the same chemistry as a 2-terminal capacitor holding ~18x today's charge per area, is rejected: its charge cannot be extracted at low field in ns (see notes).
why: Non-volatile 2-4 b/cell gain cell with 5 ns writes; refresh -> 0. Density per tier similar to a 2T0C (~10F2) but multiplied by bits per cell. Unproven endurance.

title: Nested-precision bit-plane memory + self-speculative decoding
idea: INT8/FP8 weights are quantised in a nested (Matryoshka-style) way, so the top 2 or 4 bit planes are themselves a usable low-precision model. The memory controller stores the planes in separate address ranges and streams 'planes 0-1', 'planes 0-3' or all of them, in 512 B-2 KB chunks that match DRAM bursts and pages. Decode is self-speculative: draft k tokens with the top planes only (25-50% of the weight bytes), then verify all k in one batched pass with every plane. No second model is stored.
why: 1.1-1.8x effective decode bandwidth (weight reads per accepted token 0.89-0.55), with zero extra capacity.

title: Memory interposer: oxide gain-cell tiers built into the silicon interposer
idea: Large AI packages use a silicon interposer that carries only wires and TSVs. Build 8 tiers of BEOL oxide gain cells (B3-04 coax cells, or A3-style vertical 2T0C) into the interposer's metal stack at <=400 C on the 65 nm-class line that makes interposers, with stitched periodic arrays under the GPU and HBM footprints and keep-outs around TSVs and bump fields. The GPU reads this memory straight down through its existing micro-bumps or hybrid bonds, adding a capacity tier between on-die SRAM and HBM with no extra footprint. Oxide cells hold >200 s at 95 C (imec), so the hot interposer is acceptable.
why: +21-145 GB per package on a 2,700 mm2 interposer (up to ~250 GB on 4,700 mm2) at ~0.3 pJ/bit vs 3.5 for HBM, for ~$100-240 of added tier cost per interposer.

title: Sidewall-wired DRAM cube with adaptive (die-position-corrected) side-face lithography
idea: Thin DRAM dies to 30-50 um, stack them with 2-5 um adhesive and no TSVs, then polish one or two faces of the cube to expose edge pads that each die routes to its edge. Pattern the vertical bus on the face with maskless laser direct imaging that first measures each die's actual position and adapts the wiring (adaptive patterning, as in fan-out packaging), so several um of die misplacement do not matter. Plated Cu stripes ~10 um thick carry power along the same face, and a base logic die at the bottom connects to the side bus.
why: TSV-free HBM-class stack: removes TSV keep-out and TSV/bond yield loss (HBM tax 3x -> ~2x [ESTIMATE]); 2,500-5,000 bus wires on two faces; 20-high stacks in under 1 mm.

title: Top-k KV from in-memory scoring of MSB-plane sketches
idea: Keys are quantised per channel to INT8 (KIVI-style) and stored as bit planes. The 4 MSB planes live in a PIM-capable tier (HBM-PIM or LPDDR5X-PIM). The low planes and V live in a cheaper capacity tier (LPDDR or CXL DRAM). Each decode step broadcasts the query to bank-level units, which compute approximate q.k scores from the MSB planes with bit-serial adds at the sense-amp stripe or the existing PIM MAC units, and return only scores (2 B per token per KV head). The GPU picks the top-k tokens (k ~ 1-4k) and fetches their full K and V. Nothing is stored twice: the sketch is the high planes of the real data.
why: At 128k-token contexts: ~7x less KV traffic per decode step and ~8x less HBM capacity for KV, with full KV in a ~3x cheaper-per-bit tier. In-memory scoring cuts the sketch pass's interface traffic ~2,500x.

title: MSB-DRAM: hierarchical 64-cell bitlines with sense amps bonded under the array
idea: Keep a conventional 1T1C cell (Si BCAT, or an oxide 4F2 VCT) but break each bitline into 64-cell local segments. Eight local segments in a column each connect through one pass transistor (built in the cell process) to a short global bitline that drops through a single Cu-SiCN hybrid bond to a sense amplifier on a separately made logic periphery wafer bonded face-to-face (Samsung's periphery-under-cell scheme, but at sense-amp granularity). Only the segment holding the activated wordline is switched on, so the sense amp sees ~9 fF instead of ~35 fF. By the A1 sense criterion the capacitor needed falls from 5.4 fF to ~1.4-1.8 fF, a 335-445 nm stub instead of a 1.3 um pillar; alternatively keep the tall capacitor and drop the array voltage toward ~0.4 V. Sense amps, sub-array decoders and I/O leave the cell wafer, lifting array efficiency from ~0.51 to ~0.70.
why: Capacitor aspect ratio 62 -> 16-21 (3-4x shorter, no AR-60 capacitor etch); bitline energy per sensed bit 3.9x lower at today's VARY, or ~22x lower at VARY ~0.4 V with the tall capacitor; 1.37x density from array efficiency; bond pitch 0.74-1.05 um instead of 0.26-0.37 um. Cost per bit ~1.1-1.3x 1-beta in 2D (an energy and capacitor win, not a cost win, until stacked).

title: Sequential periphery-over-cell for Si DRAM: lithographic vias instead of hybrid bonds
